lead: Computer graphics turns a numerical model into a picture. The model may be a car body, a metro line, a tumour in a scan, or a cricket ball in flight. Software computes what the picture should contain, and hardware puts coloured dots on a screen. The opposite job, starting from a picture already captured and improving or measuring it, is image processing. This chapter fixes that difference, sketches how screens moved from vector drawing to raster grids and GPUs, and surveys the main application areas.

blocks.text: Computer graphics starts with a model: numbers that describe shape, position, colour, camera and light. A car door is a set of surfaces. A metro line is a list of stations and segments. A cricket ball is a moving point with a trail. The renderer converts the model into pixel colours. The display puts those colours on the screen, one frame after another.

items: Rendering computes the colour of each pixel from the model, camera and lights.
Display stores the finished frame in a framebuffer and lights the screen.

blocks.text: A pixel is one addressable dot on the screen. Resolution is the number of pixels across and down, such as 1080 × 1920. A framebuffer is the memory that holds one frame. Colour is stored as numbers, often three bytes for red, green and blue (see colour models). A raster display refreshes a grid of pixels in order. A vector display draws only the lines in its display list (see raster versus vector graphics and display devices).

Sketchpad, built by Ivan Sutherland, is usually named as the first interactive drawing program. A user drew with a light pen and the program stored constraints, so a line stayed attached to a corner. It showed that a person could manipulate a model directly on a screen.

Early screens were vector, also called calligraphic or random scan. The electron beam moved only along the lines to be drawn. Lines were sharp, but filled areas were hard and the number of lines was limited. Raster screens won once memory became cheap. A raster screen sweeps every line, stores colours in a framebuffer, and can fill any shape. Colour depth grew from a few bits to 24 bits per pixel and beyond.

The graphics processing unit, or GPU, arrived to feed the raster screen. It has many small cores that colour vertices and fragments in parallel. Programming moved from fixed functions to shaders. APIs such as OpenGL expose this pipeline (see graphics programming with OpenGL).

CAD and product design. A bracket, a gearbox or a phone case is modelled as surfaces and solids. The designer rotates it, checks clearance, and renders a catalogue image. Modelling is heavy; rendering may be real time during design or offline for advertising.

GIS and metro maps. Roads, water lines, metro routes and stations are stored as vector data with coordinates. The renderer draws them at any zoom. A metro map is mostly vector graphics: lines, stations and labels, not a photograph.

Medicine. A CT or MRI scanner reconstructs slices from measurements. That reconstruction is image processing. Graphics then renders a 3D volume so a surgeon can plan a cut, rotate the view and see a tumour behind bone. Modelling comes from scan data, and rendering adds lights and cut planes.

Weather radar. Radar measures reflectivity, a number for each direction and range. A colour map turns those numbers into an image, and a sequence of images becomes a loop. This is visualisation: measured data in, picture out. Cleaning noise from the radar image is image processing.

Film and cricket. Film uses modelling, rendering and compositing. Cricket broadcast overlays such as a pitch map or wagon wheel are drawn from tracked ball and shot data, then rendered over the live video.

User interfaces and games. Icons, buttons and windows are small drawings. Games render a 3D scene at 30 to 120 frames per second and display it. The next frame must be ready before the screen asks for it.

figure.caption: One frame, end to end, with the worked example's own numbers. The renderer colours 2,073,600 pixels at 3 bytes each, so a frame is 6,220,800 bytes (5.9326 MiB); at 60 frames per second the display must be fed 373.248 MB/s, which is the job of the GPU.

spec.title: One frame: model to screen
spec.aria: A left-to-right pipeline: a 1080 by 1920 model goes to the renderer, which writes 3 bytes per pixel into a framebuffer holding 6,220,800 bytes (5.9326 MiB) per frame, and the display shows 60 such frames every second, a data rate of 373.248 MB per second.

examples.question: A phone screen is 1080 pixels wide and 1920 pixels high. Each pixel uses 3 bytes, one each for red, green and blue. (a) Find the bytes in one full frame, in bytes and in MiB (1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes). (b) At 60 frames per second, find the data rate in bytes per second and in MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes). (c) State one reason the phone needs a dedicated GPU.
steps: The CPU cannot prepare and push about 373 MB every second while running apps; a GPU colours pixels in parallel with a dedicated memory path and lower power.
examples.answer: One frame needs 6,220,800 bytes, about 5.9326 MiB, and 60 frames per second need 373,248,000 bytes per second, about 373.248 MB/s, so a dedicated GPU is needed.
examples.check:
w = 1080
h = 1920
bpp = 3
fps = 60
pixels = w * h
frame = pixels * bpp
mib = frame / 1048576
rate = frame * fps
mbs = rate / 1000000
print(pixels)
print(frame)
print(round(mib, 4))
print(rate)
print(round(mbs, 3))

traps: Graphics versus image processing: graphics synthesises a picture from a model; image processing starts with a captured picture and analyses or improves it. A CT reconstruction is image processing; a 3D view of the same scan is graphics.
Bytes versus bits: 3 bytes per pixel is 24 bits per pixel, not 3 bits. Frame rate multiplies bytes, not bits, unless you convert.
Model versus picture: a vector model can be rendered at any resolution; a rendered raster frame is fixed at its pixel grid. Do not say the model has pixels.
Sketchpad is usually named as the first interactive drawing program, not the first graphics program and not the first raster display.
Applications are not only film and games: CAD, GIS, medicine and weather radar are graphics too. The examiner often asks for three non-entertainment uses.

quiz.q: State the difference between computer graphics and image processing.
quiz.a: Computer graphics builds a picture from a numerical model. Image processing starts with a picture already captured and analyses or improves it.

quiz.q: Name the program usually called the first interactive drawing program.
Why did raster displays replace vector displays for general use?
quiz.a: Raster displays became cheap with memory. They store a full framebuffer, so they can fill any shape, show photographs and use many colours. Vector displays draw only lines, so filled areas are hard and the line count is limited.

quiz.q: A screen is 800 × 600 pixels and uses 4 bytes per pixel. Find the bytes per second needed at 30 frames per second, and give the answer in MB/s (1 MB = 10^6 bytes).
A metro map app stores line data as vectors and satellite photos as rasters. Which scales better when the user zooms, and why?
quiz.a: Vector line data scales better: the renderer redraws lines and labels at the new zoom, so edges stay sharp. A satellite raster has fixed pixels; zooming enlarges them and blurs the image. Practical apps show vectors over rasters.

quiz.q: A weather radar image is produced from measured reflectivity. Is this computer graphics or image processing? Explain both stages.
quiz.a: The measurement and reconstruction are data acquisition and image processing: noise is cleaned and numbers are formed. Turning reflectivity numbers into colours and drawing them on a map is computer graphics, a visualisation step. The broadcast loop then displays rendered frames.

quiz.q: In 3D surgery planning, classify the work as modelling, rendering or display.
quiz.a: Modelling: segment the scan and build surfaces or a volume. Rendering: compute a 3D view with lights and cut planes from a chosen camera. Display: show the frames on the monitor as the surgeon rotates the view.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern GPUs run general programs called shaders, so graphics code and simulation code share the same hardware. Real-time ray tracing and virtual reality push frame rate and latency, not just pixel count. Scientific visualisation turns simulation output into images, and web APIs bring the same pipeline to a browser. Search next for GPU rasterization pipeline, shader programming, volume rendering and WebGL.
